notes.meaning: Elizur, leader of the tribe of Reuben, brings his gift on the fourth day. The silver platter weighed about sixty ounces and the bowl about thirty-five. They were filled with flour and oil for a grain offering, a gift of food given to God. The small gold dish held incense, probably for the golden incense altar. Matthew Henry says it was fitting that so great a King be served with fine dishes, and that we should give our best as we are able.

A burnt offering was an animal burned whole on the altar. A sin offering was a sacrifice that dealt with sin. By bringing every kind, the leaders showed they gladly accepted the laws God had just given. Even at this happy time there is a sin offering. Henry notes that even our best service is mixed with sin, so we come to God trusting Christ as the great sin offering.

A peace offering was shared. Part of it became a meal the giver ate with friends. These had to be eaten the same day, and this amount was enough for one day's feast. Henry sees a lesson in self-control: even a holy feast should not turn into excess.

On the fifth day Shelumiel of Simeon comes. The tribes came in the same order they camped around the tabernacle. Each leader had his own day, so each tribe got equal honor. Henry compares it to Aaron's breastplate, where each tribe had its own stone.

Simeon's gift is exactly the same as the others. The leaders and tribes were probably not equally rich, yet the gifts matched. Henry says this showed that every tribe had an equal share in the altar. He adds that some think the heads of each tribe chipped in to help their leader pay for it.

The animals were clean and fit for sacrifice. The dishes were made for holy use. In one way this was like subjects bringing tribute to their king. But it was also an act of worship, showing that Israel was a holy people giving themselves to God.

Why repeat the same list again? Henry says Scripture has no empty repetitions. Each gift is written out in full so no one would feel slighted. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown adds that when these books were read aloud later, each tribe would feel a warm interest in what its own forefathers gave.

On the sixth day Eliasaph of Gad comes. Spreading the gifts over twelve days made the event last, so all Israel would notice and remember it. Henry says God's work should not be rushed. If we take our time, we will do it better.

Gad gives the same silver and gold. Henry notes that Israel could spare such riches. God fed them every day with bread from heaven, and they would soon be given the land of Canaan. The lesson is to be generous as our means allow.
The same sacrifices were offered day after day. Henry suggests this gave the priests and Levites plenty of practice. They became well trained in God's laws about sacrifices.

These leaders were the first and most eager to serve God. Henry calls this an example for people in authority. They should use their honor, power and wealth to promote the worship of God. Those who have more should do more good.

On the seventh day Elishama of Ephraim comes. Some have wondered whether this day was a Sabbath, the weekly day of rest. Adam Clarke says there is no proof it was. But even if it was, he asks, what better way to spend it than giving yourself to the Lord? Henry agrees that this holy work was fitting for a holy day.

Ephraim brings the same silver dishes and gold dish. In the Hebrew the word "shekel" is left out of the weights, but it is understood. Later the totals are added up: 2,400 shekels of silver and 120 of gold from all twelve leaders.

The same sacrifices were offered again. Henry says this shows how much God enjoys worship, and how much we should too. If God asks for special service day after day, we should not call it a chore or grow tired of doing good.

Each gift is written down with the giver's name. Henry says God carefully remembers what is given to him. He points to Jesus watching people give at the temple (Mark 12:41). Even a small gift, given as we are able, is noticed and will be rewarded.

On the eighth day Gamaliel of Manasseh comes. His name was already listed among the leaders in Numbers 1. Some tribes had more honored places in the camp. Yet Henry says all their gifts were equally welcome to God, who shows no favorites (James 2:1).
Manasseh's gift matches the rest. At the end of the chapter all the gifts are added together into a great total. Henry says this shows how rich God's house becomes when everyone does their part.
Once again come the burnt offering and the sin offering. Henry notes that God showed he accepted these gifts. At the end of the chapter he spoke with Moses as a friend from above the ark (v. 89).
Gamaliel's offering is closed with his name, as each one is. Henry says rich and poor stand alike before God. What we give him is like a loan to the Lord, and he does not forget it (Hebrews 6:10).
